BUG: LogisticRegression (and other GLMs) can silently return badly wrong coefficients on off-centered data > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact scikit-learn's linear models split into two families with very different handling of un-centered features: - `LinearRegression`, `Ridge`, `Lasso`, `ElasticNet` go through `_preprocess_data`, which centers `X` and `y` (explicitly for dense data, algebraically for sparse) before solving, then reconstructs the intercept afterward. Centering is a pure reparametrization here: for any fixed `coef`, shifting `X` by a constant only shifts the intercept, and the L1/L2 penalty doesn't touch the intercept, so the optimal `coef` is mathematically invariant to any additive shift of the features. Ridge/Lasso exploit this to shield users from poor numerical stability on high mean to variance ratio features. - `LogisticRegression`, `PoissonRegressor`, `GammaRegressor`, `TweedieRegressor` (the `LinearModelLoss` + `NewtonSolver`/lbfgs/newton-cg/newton-cholesky family) do **not** do this. The intercept is just another free parameter solved jointly with the coefficients directly on the raw `X`. There is no `_preprocess_data`-equivalent step. The same invariance holds mathematically for this second family too (same argument: additive shift + unpenalized intercept), but because nothing centers the data first, the solvers can lose that invariance numerically. Concretely: - `newton-cholesky` builds its Hessian from the raw `[X, 1]` design. Eliminating the intercept column during Cholesky factorization implicitly computes `X.T @ X - n * mean(X) * mean(X).T` which can yield catastrophic-cancellation-prone quantity. The scipy solver normally fires a warning or an error in this case, so at least, it's visible for users something is wrong. - `lbfgs` doesn't have a cancellation problem in this sense, but its gradient-norm convergence check can be satisfied prematurely on badly-offset data, silently stopping far from the true optimum, with **no warning at all**. User-facing impact: any real dataset with a feature that's far from zero-mean relative to its variance (a year, a timestamp, an age, a physical measurement with an offset unit) can silently produce badly wrong `coef_`/`intercept_` for these estimators, without any indication something went wrong. I stumbled on this while investigating numerical-stability discussions in #34793 (Ridge's cholesky centering trick). ### Steps/Code to Reproduce Sweep used to generate the plot below:
```python import warnings import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.linear_model import ( LinearRegression, LogisticRegression, Ridge, TweedieRegressor, PoissonRegressor, ElasticNet, ) def relative_error_vs_mean_variance_ratio( linear_estimator, dtype="float32", random_seed=0, max_ratio=1e5 ): rng = np.random.RandomState(random_seed) n_samples, n_features = 5000, 5 X = rng.normal(size=(n_samples, n_features)) true_coef = rng.normal(size=n_features) proba = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ true_coef))) y = (rng.uniform(size=n_samples) < proba).astype(int) X, y = X.astype(dtype), y.astype(dtype) linear_estimator.fit(X, y) ref = linear_estimator.coef_.copy() assert np.linalg.norm(ref) > 0.1 # we want coefs that aren't too small ratios = np.logspace(0, np.log10(max_ratio), num=30) errors, has_warnings = [], [] for offset in ratios: with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught: linear_estimator.fit((X + offset).astype(dtype), y) shifted = linear_estimator.coef_.copy() errors.append(np.linalg.norm(shifted - ref) / np.linalg.norm(ref)) has_warnings.append(bool(caught)) return ratios, np.array(errors), np.array(has_warnings) models = [ Ridge(solver="cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), Ridge(solver="lbfgs", positive=True, alpha=1 / 5000), ElasticNet(alpha=1 / 5000), LinearRegression(), # GLMs: LogisticRegression(solver="lbfgs"), LogisticRegression(solver="newton-cholesky"), TweedieRegressor(solver="lbfgs", alpha=1 / 5000), TweedieRegressor(solver="newton-cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), PoissonRegressor(solver="lbfgs", alpha=1 / 5000), PoissonRegressor(solver="newton-cholesky", alpha=1 / 5000), ] dtypes = ["float32", "float64"] n_cols = 2 n_rows = -(-len(models) // n_cols) # ceil division fig, axes = plt.subplots( n_rows, n_cols, figsize=(5 * n_cols, 3 * n_rows), sharex=True, sharey=True ) axes = axes.ravel() for ax, model in zip(axes, models): results = [relative_error_vs_mean_variance_ratio(model, dtype=dtype) for dtype in dtypes] for (ratios, errors, has_warnings), dtype in zip(results, dtypes): line, = ax.plot(ratios, errors, label=dtype) ax.scatter( ratios[has_warnings], errors[has_warnings], marker="x", s=10, color=line.get_color(), ) ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02) ax.set_xscale("log") ax.set_title(str(model), fontsize=9) ax.tick_params(axis="x", which="both", labelbottom=True) ax.set_xlabel("mean/variance ratio") for ax in axes[len(models):]: ax.axis("off") for ax in axes[::n_cols]: ax.set_ylabel("relative error") axes[0].legend() fig.tight_layout() ```

A blip only appears in float32 at the extreme end (ratio ≥1e4), never in float64. - `LogisticRegression`, `TweedieRegressor`, `PoissonRegressor` (bottom three rows, the GLM family), with *either* solver (lbfgs or newton-cholesky): garbage coefficients starting at a ratio as low as ~20-100 in float32 and ~300-5000 in float64. ### Versions ```shell System: python: 3.14.6 (main, Jun 23 2026, 15:18:23) [Clang 22.1.3 ] executable: /home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/bin/python machine: Linux-6.17.0-1032-oem-x86_64-with-glibc2.39 Python dependencies: sklearn: 1.10.dev0 pip: None setuptools: None numpy: 2.5.3 scipy: 1.18.1 Cython: 3.3.0 pandas: 3.0.5 matplotlib: 3.11.1 joblib: 1.6.0 threadpoolctl: 3.6.0 narwhals: 2.26.0 Built with OpenMP: True threadpoolctl info: user_api: blas internal_api: openblas num_threads: 14 prefix: libscipy_openblas filepath: /home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/lib/python3.14/site-packages/numpy.libs/libscipy_openblas64_-f48b354e.so version: 0.3.34.106.0 threading_layer: pthreads architecture: Haswell user_api: blas internal_api: openblas num_threads: 14 prefix: libscipy_openblas filepath: /home/arthur/scikit-learn/sklearn-env/lib/python3.14/site-packages/scipy.libs/libscipy_openblas-5f890258.so version: 0.3.31.dev threading_layer: pthreads architecture: Haswell user_api: openmp internal_api: openmp num_threads: 14 prefix: libgomp filepath: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libgomp.so.1.0.0 version: None ``` ### Interest in fixing the bug Yes. permutation_importance computes non-zero importance for features the model never uses when max_samples < 1

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm an undergraduate economics student at UC Davis. I use scikit-learn for data analysis and use permutation importance to understand which features matter. This is my first issue filed against scikit-learn.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

**What:** When `max_samples` is set below 1, features that the model never uses still get non-zero permutation importances. By definition, shuffling a column the model does not look at cannot change the predictions, so its importance should be exactly 0. With `max_samples=1.0` the importance is indeed 0; the problem only appears when a subsample is used.

**My example:** The model only uses feature 0; features 1 and 2 are pure noise that the model never reads. With `max_samples=0.5`, both features 1 and 2 get an importance of −0.0104. The 5 repetitions (`n_repeats=5`) return exactly the same value, so the standard deviation is 0. The bias changes in magnitude and sign with the subsample size: −0.026 at 0.2 and +0.006 at 0.1. This shows it is sampling noise, not a real feature contribution.

**Cause** (I read `sklearn/inspection/_permutation_importance.py`): The baseline score is computed on all rows, while the shuffled score is computed on the subsampled rows only, and the two are subtracted. The difference therefore mixes in the gap between the full-data score and the subsample score, which has nothing to do with the feature. The docstring says a fresh sample is drawn for each repetition; in practice the subsample is drawn once per feature before the repetitions, and all features share the same random seed — so repeating does not average the bias away (std = 0), and every irrelevant feature gets the same bias.

**Impact on users:** `max_samples` exists to save time on large datasets. With this bug, irrelevant features get spuriously positive or negative importances, which can make them look useful or harmful, and can also corrupt feature ranking.

**AI usage disclosure:** I used an AI assistant to help identify this problem and write the reproduction script. The description above is my own, and the reproduction was run on my own computer.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np, sklearn
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score
print(sklearn.__version__)
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
n = 200
X = rng.randn(n, 3)
y = 3 * X[:, 0] + rng.randn(n)          # only feature 0 matters
X[:, 1:] = rng.randn(n, 2)                # features 1, 2: pure noise
model = LinearRegression().fit(X[:, :1], y)  # model uses ONLY feature 0 ...
class OnlyFirst:                              # ... wrapped so it accepts 3 columns
    def fit(self, X, y): return self
    def predict(self, X): return model.predict(X[:, :1])
    def score(self, X, y): return r2_score(y, self.predict(X))
est = OnlyFirst()

r = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=0.5, random_state=0)
print("importances_mean (max_samples=0.5):", r.importances_mean)
print("importances (features 1,2 are ignored by the model, so must be exactly 0):")
print(r.importances[1:])

# Independent expectation: permuting a column the model never reads cannot change
# predictions, so the permuted score equals the score on the SAME rows -> importance 0.
r_full = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=1.0, random_state=0)
print("importances_mean (max_samples=1.0):", r_full.importances_mean)
print("baseline (all rows) r2:", r2_score(y, est.predict(X)))
for ms in (0.2, 0.1):
    r = permutation_importance(est, X, y, n_repeats=5, max_samples=ms, random_state=0)
    print(f"max_samples={ms}: importances_mean =", r.importances_mean, " importances_std =", r.importances_std)
```

For every repetition, the importances of features 1 and 2 should be exactly 0 — identical to the result with `max_samples=1.0`.

BUG fetch_file(url, folder=...) crashes with confusing FileNotFoundError instead of creating the directory

### Describe the bug

`sklearn.datasets.fetch_file(url, folder=...)` raises a confusing, low-level `FileNotFoundError` instead of creating the target directory when the caller passes an explicit `folder` that doesn't exist yet.

The docstring for `folder` doesn't state that the directory must already exist:

> `folder` : str or Path, default=None
> Directory to save the file to. If None, the file is downloaded in a folder with a name derived from the URL host name and path under scikit-learn data home folder.

But directory creation only happens for the *default* case:

https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/datasets/_base.py#L1639-L1642

```python
if folder is None:
    folder = Path(get_data_home()) / folder_from_url
    makedirs(folder, exist_ok=True)
```

`makedirs(..., exist_ok=True)` is nested inside `if folder is None:`, so it only runs when `fetch_file` derives the folder itself. When the caller explicitly passes `folder=`, no directory creation happens at all. Downstream, `_fetch_remote` (same file, around line 1502) does:

```python
temp_file = NamedTemporaryFile(
    prefix=remote.filename + ".part_", dir=folder_path, delete=False
)
```

which raises `FileNotFoundError` if `folder_path` doesn't exist — an opaque, low-level crash referencing an internal `.part_...` temp-file name that the user never specified, rather than a clear message about the missing directory.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_file

# Using a local file:// URL as the "remote" source, no network required.
src_file = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "source.csv"
src_file.write_text("a,b,c\n1,2,3\n")
url = "file://localhost" + str(src_file)

target_dir = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "does_not_exist_yet"
print("target_dir exists before:", target_dir.exists())

fetch_file(url, folder=target_dir)
```

### Expected Results

Either the directory gets created (matching what already happens for the default `folder=None` case — verified working), or a clear, actionable error naming the missing directory.

For comparison, the default-folder path already creates the directory transparently and succeeds:
```python
result = fetch_file(url)  # folder=None (default)
print(result, result.exists())  # succeeds, directory auto-created
```

### Actual Results

```
target_dir exists before: False
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/.../does_not_exist_yet/source.csv.part_1flw14k2'
```

### Versions

Reproduced on current `main`, no network access required (repro uses a local `file://` URL). This appears to have existed since `fetch_file` was introduced (#29354) — no prior discussion of this specific asymmetry found.

---

I dug into this while looking for an unrelated fix and haven't opened a PR — the obvious fix is to move (or duplicate) the `makedirs(folder, exist_ok=True)` call so it also runs for a caller-supplied `folder`, mirroring the default-path behavior. Happy to put a PR together if that direction looks right to a maintainer.

[BUG] RidgeClassifierCV(scoring="accuracy", cv=None) returns incorrect best_score_ for binary classification

### Introduce yourself

hello, I am a professor of computer science and a core developer at [aeon ](https://github.com/aeon-toolkit/aeon). We use RidgeClassifierCV as a classifier head for many of our transformation based pipelines and ensembles, particularly the convolution based ones, and this bug was found by our core dev Matthew (@MatthewMiddlehurst) when reviewing [this PR] (https://github.com/aeon-toolkit/aeon/pull/3655) that adapted one of these pipeline classifiers, the Arsenal, which is a component of our HIVE-COTEv2 classifier and is one of my finest moments in algorithm naming :) 

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`RidgeClassifierCV(scoring="accuracy", cv=None)` computes an incorrect best_score_ for binary classification problems: it always returns accuracy of 1.0, even when the problem contains substantial label noise and the fitted classifier is clearly not perfect.

We use best_score_ as an estimate of each ensemble member's classification accuracy and use it as an ensemble weight. For multiclass problems this appears to work as expected. For binary problems, however, all ensemble members receive a weight of 1.0, effectively disabling the weighting mechanism.

The behaviour appears specific to the default cv=None path. Using an explicit cross-validation splitter such as cv=5 gives plausible accuracy scores.

Looking at the implementation, the cause may be the classification scoring code in the GCV path reconstructing class labels using `y.argmax(axis=1)`. For binary classification, LabelBinarizer produces a single-column target, so argmax(axis=1) is always zero.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeClassifierCV
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
X = rng.normal(size=(200, 20))
y = rng.randint(0, 2, size=200)

clf_loo = RidgeClassifierCV( alphas=[0.1, 1.0, 10.0], scoring="accuracy", ).fit(X, y)
clf_cv = RidgeClassifierCV( alphas=[0.1, 1.0, 10.0], scoring="accuracy", cv=5, ).fit(X, y)
print("cv=None best_score_:", clf_loo.best_score_)
print("cv=5 best_score_:", clf_cv.best_score_)
print("training accuracy:", clf_loo.score(X, y))

import sklearn;
sklearn.show_versions()
```
Outputs
```python
cv=None best_score_: 1.0
cv=5 best_score_: 0.515
training accuracy: 0.65
```
on random data. 

### Expected Results

an estimate of accuracy specific to the training data, not always 1.0.

chatgpt traced this back and thinks it was introduced in 0.23 by PR #14848, merged on 6 January 2020. I have not verified this myself.

### Actual Results

For binary classification with cv=None, best_score_ is always reported as 1.0

balanced_accuracy_score(adjusted=True) returns -inf when a single class survives the NaN filter

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm a data scientist in Toronto working on forecasting and causal inference. I've recently started contributing to scikit-learn — I have an open PR at #34888 (array API support for ShrunkCovariance) — and I found this while looking into #33712, where I was trying to work out which of two distinct undefined cases in balanced_accuracy_score that issue refers to. This one turned out to be independent of it, so I'm filing it separately.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

balanced_accuracy_score(..., adjusted=True) returns -inf when a single class survives the internal NaN filter. The adjusted score is bounded — it spans [-1, 1], reaching -1 only at n_classes=2 — so -inf is outside the documented range of the metric.

This surfaces in cross-validation on small or imbalanced folds, where a fold can easily contain a single class. One -inf propagates through any mean over folds, turning the whole aggregate into -inf and silently destroying an otherwise valid CV score. The related nan case is at least absorbed by nan-aware aggregation; -inf is not.

Mechanism: n_classes is read after the NaN filter at _classification.py:2940, so when one class survives, chance = 1 / 1 and `score /= 1 - chance` at line 2946 divides by zero. The np.errstate guard wraps the per-class division only, not this one, and has been scoped that way since the original commit (e888c0d65cf, "ENH multiclass balanced accuracy" #10587, 2018) — the guard and the unguarded division were introduced together.

This is separate from #33712: it predates it and reproduces without touching replace_undefined_by.


### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.metrics import balanced_accuracy_score

# Case 1
print(balanced_accuracy_score([0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0], adjusted=True))

# Case 2
print(balanced_accuracy_score([0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], adjusted=True))
```

## Expected Results

A value within the documented range of the adjusted metric, [-1, 1]. A score documented as bounded should not return -inf.

## Actual Results

On scikit-learn 1.9.0 (installed from PyPI), case 1 returns nan:

```
/tmp/sk19/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py:614: UserWarning: A single label was found in 'y_true' and 'y_pred'. For the confusion matrix to have the correct shape, use the 'labels' parameter to pass all known labels.
  warnings.warn(
/tmp/sk19/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py:2946: RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in scalar divide
  score /= 1 - chance
nan
```

Handle new `pd.StringDtype` that is coming in pandas 3

This issue is the result of investigating https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/31778

The failures in the nightlies are due to changes coming in pandas 3.0. In particular the switch to using `StringDtype` as the type for string columns. The old behaviour was to use `object`.

This has a few effects:
- can no longer use `np.issubdtype` because the new dtype isn't one known to numpy
- selecting columns in `ColumnTransformer` doesn't select the right columns anymore

These are the failing tests:
```
FAILED compose/tests/test_column_transformer.py::test_make_column_transformer_pandas - TypeError: Cannot interpret '<StringDtype(storage='python', na_value=nan)>'...
FAILED compose/tests/test_column_transformer.py::test_column_transformer_remainder_pandas[pd-index-expected_cols4] - TypeError: Cannot interpret '<StringDtype(storage='python', na_value=nan)>'...
FAILED compose/tests/test_column_transformer.py::test_make_column_selector_with_select_dtypes[cols1-None-None-object] - AssertionError: 
FAILED compose/tests/test_column_transformer.py::test_make_column_selector_with_select_dtypes[cols3-None-include3-None] - AssertionError: 
FAILED compose/tests/test_column_transformer.py::test_make_column_selector_with_select_dtypes[cols4-None-object-None] - AssertionError: 
FAILED compose/tests/test_column_transformer.py::test_make_column_selector_with_select_dtypes[cols12-None-include12-None] - AssertionError: 
FAILED compose/tests/test_column_transformer.py::test_column_transformer_with_make_column_selector - AssertionError: 
FAILED preprocessing/tests/test_encoders.py::test_encoder_dtypes_pandas - assert False
FAILED preprocessing/tests/test_function_transformer.py::test_function_transformer_with_dataframe_and_check_inverse_True - TypeError: Cannot interpret '<StringDtype(storage='python', na_value=nan)>'...
```

Three of these (first one and last two) are due to using `issubdtype`. The other failures are due to not selecting the right columns (n.b. the way the test is written the "desired" and "actual" are swapped in the error message, I think)


## Potential Fixes

Code that works both with old and new versions of pandas. One PR to address the `issubdtype` problem and one to address column selector logic.

Instances where we use `issubdtype` probably need to gain a special handling for the possibility of the new dtype.

For the `ColumnSelector` test failures we need to investigate how much of this is due to how the tests are written and how much due to real changes. For example, it could be that updating the tests to be "written for the new string dtype" means they will pass. This means the problem is using a mix of old and new. The fix for this is different to having to write column selector code that works with both.

## Notes

General notes on transitioning to the new string dtype https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/user_guide/migration-3-strings.html

An example of the column selector code that needs updating:
```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd  # pandas 2.3 works for seeing this

# Old behaviour
X_df = pd.DataFrame(
            {
                "col_int": np.array([0, 1, 2], dtype=int),
                "col_float": np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0], dtype=float),
                "col_str": ["one", "two", "three"],
            },
            columns=["col_int", "col_float", "col_str"],
        )

X_df.select_dtypes(include=[np.number, object])
#    col_int  col_float col_str
#0        0        0.0     one
#1        1        1.0     two
#2        2        2.0   three

#####
# New behaviour
pd.options.future.infer_string = True

X_df = pd.DataFrame(
            {
                "col_int": np.array([0, 1, 2], dtype=int),
                "col_float": np.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0], dtype=float),
                "col_str": ["one", "two", "three"],
            },
            columns=["col_int", "col_float", "col_str"],
        )

# Selects one fewer column
X_df.select_dtypes(include=[np.number, object])
#   col_int  col_float
#0        0        0.0
#1        1        1.0
#2        2        2.0
```

Improve sample_weight handling in sag(a)

### Describe the bug

This may be more of a discussion, but overall I am not sure what treatment of weighting would preserve the convergence guarantees for the SAG(A) solver. So far as I see it, at each update step we uniformly select some index $i_j$ such that the update steps can be generalised as:

$x^{k+1} = x^{k} - \sum_{j=1}^{k} \alpha_{j} S(j, i_{1:k}) f'_{i_j}(x^j)$

Where $S(j, i_{1:k}) = 1/n$ if $j$ is the maximum iteration at which $i_j$ is selected. 

For frequency based weighting, one could sample $i_j$ using weights as a probability, and under non-uniform sampling the SAG(A) convergence guarantees still seem to hold, (see [here]([https://inria.hal.science/hal-00860051/document])).

 Alternatively as currently done, the weights could be multiplied through with the gradient update and that could also work, however I am not sure which method is best (we also here need to additionally consider the division by the cardinality of the set of "seen" elements within each update step).

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import kstest
from sklearn.linear_model.tests.test_sag import sag, squared_dloss
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
from sklearn.utils._testing import assert_allclose_dense_sparse

step_size=0.01
alpha=1

n_features = 1

rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
X, y = make_regression(n_samples=10000,random_state=77,n_features=n_features)
weights = rng.randint(0,5,size=X.shape[0])

X_repeated = np.repeat(X,weights,axis=0)
y_repeated = np.repeat(y,weights,axis=0)

weights_w_all = np.zeros([n_features,100])
weights_r_all = np.zeros([n_features,100])

for random_state in np.arange(100):

    weights_w, int_w = sag(X,y,step_size=step_size,alpha=alpha,sample_weight=weights,dloss=squared_dloss,random_state=random_state)
    weights_w_all[:,random_state] = weights_w
    weights_r, int_r = sag(X_repeated,y_repeated,step_size=step_size,alpha=alpha,dloss=squared_dloss,random_state=random_state)
    weights_r_all[:,random_state] = weights_r

print(kstest(weights_r_all[0],weights_w_all[0]))
```

note that I modified ```sag``` in test_sag.py to accept random_state:

```python
def sag(
    X,
    y,
    step_size,
    alpha,
    n_iter=1,
    dloss=None,
    sparse=False,
    sample_weight=None,
    fit_intercept=True,
    saga=False,
    random_state=77,
):
    n_samples, n_features = X.shape[0], X.shape[1]

    weights = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    sum_gradient = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    gradient_memory = np.zeros((n_samples, n_features))

    intercept = 0.0
    intercept_sum_gradient = 0.0
    intercept_gradient_memory = np.zeros(n_samples)

    rng = np.random.RandomState(random_state)
    decay = 1.0
    seen = set()

    # sparse data has a fixed decay of .01
    if sparse:
        decay = 0.01

    for epoch in range(n_iter):
        for k in range(n_samples):
            #if sample_weight is not None:
            #    idx = rng.choice(np.arange(n_samples),p=sample_weight/np.sum(sample_weight))
            #else:
            idx = int(rng.rand()*n_samples)
            # idx = k
            entry = X[idx]
            seen.add(idx)
            p = np.dot(entry, weights) + intercept
            gradient = dloss(p, y[idx])
            if sample_weight is not None:
                gradient *= sample_weight[idx]
            update = entry * gradient + alpha * weights
            gradient_correction = update - gradient_memory[idx]
            sum_gradient += gradient_correction
            gradient_memory[idx] = update
            if saga:
                weights -= gradient_correction * step_size * (1 - 1.0 / len(seen))

            if fit_intercept:
                gradient_correction = gradient - intercept_gradient_memory[idx]
                intercept_gradient_memory[idx] = gradient
                intercept_sum_gradient += gradient_correction
                gradient_correction *= step_size * (1.0 - 1.0 / len(seen))
                if saga:
                    intercept -= (
                        step_size * intercept_sum_gradient / len(seen) * decay
                    ) + gradient_correction
                else:
                    intercept -= step_size * intercept_sum_gradient / len(seen) * decay

            weights -= step_size * sum_gradient / len(seen)

    return weights, intercept
```

### Expected Results

kstest should have p-value larger than 0.025

### Actual Results

```
KstestResult(statistic=np.float64(0.44), pvalue=np.float64(4.414205948474835e-09), statistic_location=np.float64(24.644506472064027), statistic_sign=np.int8(-1))
```

With an example histogram of:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a3081d21-4ac9-491a-a437-e4f916b862b9)

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.12.4 | packaged by conda-forge | (main, Jun 17 2024, 10:13:44) [Clang 16.0.6 ]
executable: /Users/shrutinath/micromamba/envs/scikit-learn/bin/python

UX `CalibrationDisplay`'s naive use can lead to very confusing results

The naive use of `CalibrationDisplay` parameter silently leads to degenerate, noisy results when some bins have with a few data points.

For instance, look at the variability obtained by displaying for calibration curve of a fitted model evaluated on various resampling with 50 data points in total using the uniform strategy when using `n_bins=10` and the default `strategy="uniform"`:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0a925e43-0466-47aa-b57b-519da3b61b5a)


<details>

```python
# %%
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.calibration import CalibrationDisplay
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split


X, y = make_classification(n_samples=10_000, n_features=200, random_state=42)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2)

# %%
clf = LogisticRegression(C=10).fit(X_train, y_train)
# %%

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for seed in range(5):
    # resample the test set
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    indices = rng.choice(X_test.shape[0], size=50, replace=True)
    X_test_sample = X_test[indices]
    y_test_sample = y_test[indices]
    CalibrationDisplay.from_estimator(clf, X_test_sample, y_test_sample, n_bins=10, ax=ax, label=None)
```

</details>


This problem can easily happen with the default `strategy="uniform"` if the test data is not large enough. I think this class should warn the user whenever it generates bins with lower than 10 data points per bin.

A typical user will only get one of the curves above and not suspect that it's just noise without manually plotting the others by random resampling. Note that I chose a minimal test set to make the problem catastrophic above, but it can happen with larger sample sizes, in particular with the uniform strategy, in particular on imbalanced datasets.

## Updated recommendations

EDIT: based on the discussion below, here are my recommendations to address this issue:

- display a confidence interval by default to reflect our uncertainty on the calibration curve estimate (using the Clopper-Pearson analytical CI from scipy looks both reliable and cheap to compute)
- we set `n_bins=15` by default but also introduce `min_samples_per_bins=50` to automatically merge the smallest pair of neighboring bins until that constraint it met.
- we would not warn, unless the resulting merging leads to less than 3 bins for instance,
- we could keep `strategy="uniform"` if we like, but I wouldn't mind switching to `"quantile"` either.

## Original description and suggestion

In such cases, this warning could recommend to:

- use `strategy="quantile"` (which is a bit less likely to generate near empty, unstable bins);
- decrease the number of bins;
- increase the number of data points in the test set.
  
Beyond warnings, we could also offer the user extra-options to assess the stability of the calibration curve.

There are two cases:

- for a fixed trained estimator, we could estimate the uncertainty in the estimation of its calibration curve induced by the finite size of the evaluation set (irrespective of whether the training procedure is stable or not) by resampling the test set (with replacement):

```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for seed in range(10):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    indices = rng.choice(X_test.shape[0], size=X_test.shape[0], replace=True)
    X_test_resampled = X_test[indices]
    y_test_resampled = y_test[indices]

    CalibrationDisplay.from_estimator(
        clf,
        X_test_resampled,
        y_test_resampled,
        strategy="quantile",
        n_bins=10,
        ax=ax,
        label=None,
    )
```
 We could optionally offer an option to aggregate those curves by displaying a shaded region derived from the vertical quantiles (e.g. 0.05-0.95) of the interpolated y-curve values at a fine grid of x values. See also the related issue on sampling uncertainties in performance curves: #25856.

- to assess the uncertainty of the calibration of a full fitting procedure (uncertainty induced by both the finite training set size, the training algorithm itself (impacted by the choice of hyperparams) and the finite evaluation set size), we could also offer to plot calibration curves from CV results (see #21211 to implement `CalibratedDisplayCV.from_cv_results`). 


On the opposite, if all the bins have more than 1000 data points and `n_bins <= 10`, we could suggest the user to increase n_bins to 10 or more to get a finer estimation of the calibration curve. Maybe this recommendation is better to be set in a docstring rather than a warning.


I think we could start simple by opening a first PR to issue warnings for the nearly empty bin problem (with an option to silence them).

DOC: RFECV per-split ranking and support shapes omit the feature axis

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

The [`RFECV` API reference](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.feature_selection.RFECV.html) documents both `cv_results_["split(k)_ranking"]` and `cv_results_["split(k)_support"]` as arrays with shape `(n_subsets_of_features,)`.

Both arrays actually have shape `(n_subsets_of_features, n_features)`, where `n_features` is the number of original input features, `X.shape[1]`. Each row contains a rank or a selection indicator for every original feature. In contrast, `split(k)_test_score` has one scalar per evaluated subset and correctly has shape `(n_subsets_of_features,)`.

### User-facing impact

The documented shape can mislead users interpreting per-fold rankings or selection masks, for example when examining feature-selection stability. Indexing a ranking/support result by subset returns a vector over original features, not a scalar. Code written around the documented one-dimensional structure could therefore use the wrong indexing or aggregation.

This is a documentation mismatch. The reproducer does not show incorrect feature selection, scores, or predictions, and no change to the returned arrays is requested.

### Minimal reproducer

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_selection import RFECV
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

X = np.column_stack(
    (np.arange(10.), np.tile([0., 1.], 5), np.ones(10))
)
selector = RFECV(
    Ridge(), cv=2, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error"
).fit(X, np.arange(10.))

for key in ("split0_ranking", "split0_support", "split0_test_score"):
    print(key, selector.cv_results_[key].shape)

assert selector.cv_results_["split0_ranking"].shape == (3, 3)
assert selector.cv_results_["split0_support"].shape == (3, 3)
assert selector.cv_results_["split0_test_score"].shape == (3,)
```

### Observed shapes

```text
split0_ranking (3, 3)
split0_support (3, 3)
split0_test_score (3,)
```

The assertions pass. There are three evaluated subset sizes and three original features.

### Verification scope

Runtime observation: scikit-learn 1.9.0, NumPy 2.5.2, and Python 3.14.7.

The affected `/1.9/` documentation page was inspected on September 11, 2026 and was labelled 1.9.1. The documentation version and tested runtime version are distinct: the 1.9.1 runtime was not tested for this report.

The [1.9.0 implementation](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py) also explains the feature axis: it collects rankings and supports over folds, evaluated subsets, and original features, then indexes out the fold axis when assigning each per-split result.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Update the two shape annotations in the `RFECV` class docstring in [`sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py`](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/feature_selection/_rfe.py):

```diff
-        split(k)_ranking : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features,)
+        split(k)_ranking : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features, n_features)

-        split(k)_support : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features,)
+        split(k)_support : ndarray of shape (n_subsets_of_features, n_features)
```

Please also clarify the axis meanings in the descriptions:

- Rows correspond to the evaluated subset sizes, ordered consistently with `cv_results_["n_features"]`.
- Columns correspond to the original input features, in their original order. This axis does not shrink as features are eliminated and is not the final selected-feature count, `n_features_`.

For example, `cv_results_["split0_support"][i, j]` indicates whether original feature `j` was selected for the subset represented by row `i` in split 0.

The Notes paragraph also describes the "size" of every `cv_results_` array using the subset-count formula. Consider calling this the **length of the first axis** instead, since the ranking and support arrays are two-dimensional.

This request concerns the docstring and generated API reference only; the existing two-dimensional outputs should remain unchanged.

DOC/ENH: StandardScaler silently sets scale to 1.0 for zero-variance features with no warning

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm a recent CS/AI graduate currently building a personal finance app that uses scikit-learn for some ML-based features (budgeting insights, basic predictive modeling). While setting up a local editable build to start learning the codebase and look for ways to contribute, I was testing edge cases with StandardScaler and noticed it silently returns a scale of 1.0 for zero-variance features (e.g. a single-sample fit) without any warning or documentation of this behavior. I dug into the source (_handle_zeros_in_scale) to confirm it was intentional rather than a bug, and found the public docstring doesn't mention it.

I'd like to help fix this if it's something the maintainers agree is worth addressing — happy to work on either a documentation update or a warning, whichever direction you'd prefer.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

StandardScaler.fit() silently returns a scale of 1.0 (instead of erroring or
warning) when a feature has zero or near-zero variance — e.g. a single-sample
fit, or a constant column. This is implemented via the internal
_handle_zeros_in_scale helper, but the behavior is not mentioned in the
public StandardScaler docstring or the User Guide.

Minimal reproduction:

​```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[1, 2, 3]])  # single sample — zero variance
scaler = StandardScaler()
print(scaler.fit_transform(X))
# Output: [[0., 0., 0.]] — no warning, no error raised
​```

This could silently mask real data problems — e.g. an accidental single-row
fit, or a constant column slipping through a preprocessing pipeline —
producing all-zero output with no signal to the user that something
unusual happened.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Adding a note to the StandardScaler docstring (and the corresponding section of the User Guide at doc/modules/preprocessing.rst) explaining that when a feature has zero or near-zero variance, its scale_ is set to 1.0 rather than raising an error or leaving a zero — so the transformed output for that feature will be 0. rather than NaN or inf. This would at least make the existing behavior discoverable without changing any code.

Clarify parameter/hyperparameter terminology in the cross-validation workflow diagram

### Introduce yourself

I teach machine learning engineering to people who are new to machine learning.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

I use `GridSearchCV` to help learners understand grid search, model selection, and good practice. I think it is a fantastic teaching tool, and the user guide is excellent.

I've taught this section several times and have repeatedly needed to explain why the diagram says "parameters" when we are discussing hyperparameters. This is a recurring point of confusion in my teaching, which prompted this issue.

The overall workflow diagram in the cross-validation user guide uses the labels **"Parameters"** and **"Best parameters"**.

User guide:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/cross_validation.html

Direct link to the diagram:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/_images/grid_search_workflow.png

My learners are meeting the terms "parameter" and "hyperparameter" for the first time. They are still learning the difference between settings we specify or search over, such as a decision tree's maximum depth, and values the model learns during fitting.

When I explain grid search, I describe it as comparing hyperparameter settings. The diagram calls these "Parameters" and "Best parameters". I then have to explain why the same settings are being called by two different names, while learners are still trying to understand what those names mean.

I understand that scikit-learn uses "parameters" for estimator constructor settings. The glossary explains this convention:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/glossary.html#term-parameter

The cross-validation guide also uses the word "hyperparameters". A short explanation at the diagram would help beginners connect the two terms.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Could a short note be added beside or below the diagram to explain how "parameters" relates to "hyperparameters"? For example:

> Here, "parameters" means configurable estimator settings. These can include machine-learning hyperparameters, such as a decision tree's `max_depth`, as well as other configuration choices, such as which estimator or pipeline step to use. They are different from values learned by the model during fitting.

The note could link to the glossary:
https://scikit-learn.org/stable/glossary.html#term-parameter

Documentation: Incorrect description of statistic computed by MaxAbsScaler.partial_fit


> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

Hi, I’m Pradip, a Computer Engineering student and I’m currently learning and working with Python and machine learning. I use scikit-learn for learning and implementing machine learning algorithms and preprocessing techniques.

While going through the `MaxAbsScaler` documentation and source code, I noticed a discrepancy in the `partial_fit()` docstring. I’m opening this issue to clarify the documentation and make it consistent with the actual implementation.


### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

The `X` parameter description in `MaxAbsScaler.partial_fit()` currently states that the data is used to compute the **"per-feature minimum and maximum"**.

However, `MaxAbsScaler` computes the **maximum absolute value** for each feature and stores it in `max_abs_`.

For example:

```python
X = [[-2, 5],
     [-3, 1]]
```

For the first feature:

```text
minimum = -3
maximum = -2
maximum absolute value = 3
```

`MaxAbsScaler` uses `3` as the scaling value. It does not use the minimum and maximum as separate statistics.

The implementation reflects this:

```python
max_abs = xpx.nanmax(xp.abs(X), axis=0, xp=xp)
```

Therefore, the current wording may confuse users into thinking that `MaxAbsScaler` computes and uses both the minimum and maximum values independently.

This also appears inconsistent with the class-level documentation, which describes the scaler in terms of the **maximum absolute value**.

I believe this is a documentation-only issue and does not require any change to the underlying algorithm.


### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

I suggest updating the `X` parameter description in `MaxAbsScaler.partial_fit()` from:

```text
The data used to compute the per-feature minimum and maximum
used for later scaling along the features axis.
```

to:

```text
The data used to compute the per-feature maximum absolute value
used for later scaling along the features axis.
```

This would make the `partial_fit()` documentation accurately reflect the statistic computed by the implementation and remain consistent with the class-level documentation.

SelectFromModel's `prefit` fails unless fit is called when set_output(transform="pandas")

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

My understanding is that if `prefit`is true, one could, in principle call `transform()` without calling `fit()` first.

While this is true if we don't set the output to pandas, it fails when we do so:

Minimal reproduction:

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectFromModel

X, y = load_iris(as_frame=True, return_X_y=True)
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X, y)

# prefit=True -- docs say we don't need to call .fit() on sel
sel = SelectFromModel(clf, prefit=True).set_output(transform="pandas")

sel.transform(X)
```

```
NotFittedError: This SelectFromModel instance is not fitted yet. Call 'fit' with appropriate arguments before using this estimator.
```

Without `.set_output(transform="pandas")`, the identical `prefit=True` selector transforms `X` just fine with no `.fit()` call. 

The error only appears once pandas output is requested, because `set_output` internally calls `get_feature_names_out()`, which checks whether the *wrapper itself* has been fitted (via `check_is_fitted(self)`, not `check_is_fitted(self.estimator)`). 

According to Claude, that check was intentionally added in #25308 to standardize `get_feature_names_out()` behavior across `SelectorMixin` estimators.

So my question is: is this expected behaviour? or is it an unintended bug? 

From a user perspective, if I use `fit`again, even though prefit is True, I get the impression that my estimator would be re-fitted, so if this is intended, it might be worth adding a line in the docs.

```python
sel.fit(X, y)     # with prefit=True, does NOT retrain clf -- just
                  # deep-copies it and records feature_names_in_
sel.transform(X)  # now works
```

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

SelectFromModel's prefit parameter is documented as:

prefit : bool, default=False
Whether a prefit model is expected to be passed into the constructor directly or not. If True, estimator must be a fitted estimator. If False, estimator is fitted and updated by calling fit and partial_fit, respectively.

Maybe it's just me, but I sort of read this as, if the estimator is prefit, I could avoid calling fit and it would be just fine.

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Add a note to the prefit parameter docstring, e.g.:

Note: even with prefit=True, .fit() must still be called before using get_feature_names_out() or set_output(transform="pandas"), since these check whether the selector itself (not the underlying estimator) has been fitted. Calling .fit() in this case does not refit estimator; it only records bookkeeping metadata (estimator_, feature_names_in_).

BIC-based model selection in plot_gmm_selection.py silently picks the wrong model under anisotropy severe enough to break its own initialization

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

## Describe the issue linked to the documentation

`examples/mixture/plot_gmm_selection.py` demonstrates using `GridSearchCV` + BIC to select `n_components` and `covariance_type` for a `GaussianMixture`. It works well on the example's data because the two components are already well separated relative to their own spread, so `GaussianMixture`'s default k-means-style initialization lands close to the true partition and EM refines it correctly.

As in [#34842](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34842), that init dependency is invisible in the example and doesn't generalize. If the true clusters are anisotropic enough that Euclidean-distance-based initialization is already unreliable, BIC does not fail loudly -- it fails silently, by scoring every candidate in the grid on a bad fit and confidently reporting the best of a bad set. A reader walks away with "BIC picked `n_components=2`, full covariance, done" with no signal that a different initialization would have picked a different, better-scoring model entirely.

Concretely, on two anisotropic "parallel cigars" clusters (`make_blobs` + a linear `transformation`, same construction as [#34842](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34842), ratio 4x rather than 80x), the grid search over `n_components` and `covariance_type` with default initialization selects a 3-component model, when the true generative model has 2 components. The 2-component model is available in the same search space -- it's just never found, because every restart of k-means++ on this data lands in roughly the same wrong place.

## Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Add a new section to `plot_gmm_selection.py`, after the existing example, showing:

1. The same "parallel cigars" dataset as [#34842](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34842), where default (raw) k-means-style initialization for `GaussianMixture` gives a partition bad enough that BIC-based model selection lands on the wrong `n_components`.
2. A whitened-init variant: use `PCA(whiten=True)` + `KMeans` only to get an initial cluster assignment, derive `weights_init`/`means_init` from that assignment on the raw data, then fit and score every model (whitened-init or not) by BIC on the raw data. This keeps the BIC comparison valid while showing that whitening the initialization -- not the model itself -- restores the correct selection.

Draft implementation, for review before opening a PR: https://github.com/jovo/scikit-learn/pull/2 (this is a fork-internal PR against my own fork, not yet a real PR against `scikit-learn/scikit-learn` -- opening one once there's agreement this is worth doing, per the guidance on [#34842](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34842)).

GaussianMixture is not a universal fix for anisotropy — plot_kmeans_assumptions.py doesn't show the case where whitening is needed too

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

`examples/cluster/plot_kmeans_assumptions.py` shows `KMeans` failing on anisotropic blobs and proposes `GaussianMixture` as the fix, since it fits a full covariance per component instead of assuming spherical clusters.

That's correct for the anisotropy shown in the example, but not universally: `GaussianMixture` is still initialized from a k-means-style partition of the raw data, and EM only ever *refines* that partition rather than searching from scratch. If the anisotropy is severe enough, the initial partition can already be too wrong for EM to recover from, even with unconstrained covariances.

**What a reader might do without knowing this:** someone hits poor `KMeans` results on their own anisotropic data, finds this example, and takes away the rule "if k-means struggles with anisotropy, switch to `GaussianMixture`." They swap it in, `GaussianMixture` returns *some* clustering with no error or warning, and they ship it — never realizing the result can be arbitrarily wrong, because their anisotropy happened to be severe enough to also break the initialization this fix silently depends on. Nothing in the current example signals that this failure mode exists, so there's no reason for them to suspect it.

I'd like to propose adding: a more severely anisotropic dataset (built the same way as the file's existing `X_aniso` — `make_blobs` + a linear `transformation`, just more extreme) where `GaussianMixture` fails (ARI ≈ 0), and where whitening first with `PCA(whiten=True)` fixes it (ARI ≈ 0.9+) — no custom clustering code needed, just a change of input to the same `GaussianMixture` call.

(Caveat: this degrades in high dimension too — same construction at d=30, ARI drops back to ≈0.)

Draft implementation, kept up to date: jovo/scikit-learn#1 (opened against my own fork so it stays open and reviewable rather than getting auto-closed like a direct PR here would while this issue is pending triage — happy to open a PR against this repo once there's agreement this is worth doing).

Investigation: conda-forge scikit-learn slower than PyPI (ExtraTrees case)

While looking at [builds comparison results](https://probabl-ai.github.io/scikit-learn-benchmarks/builds_comparison.html) from my benchmarks (https://github.com/probabl-ai/scikit-learn-benchmarks), I noticed `ExtraTrees*.fit` was often ~25% slower on conda-forge builds of
scikit-learn 1.9.0 than on PyPI wheels.

Two distinct bugs were found along the way; only the second one explains the slowdown:

1. **O3 vs O2** (documented in #34865): `-O3` in meson doesn't survive an environment `CFLAGS` that also sets `-O2` (which conda-forge's compiler activation does).

2. **Version of `glibc`** (cause of the slowdown): conda-forge compiles scikit-learn against a `sysroot_linux-64=2.17` (glibc 2.17, from 2012-12-25). That old glibc's `<math.h>` defines the `isnan()` macro as a dispatch to glibc-internal `__isnanf`/`__isnan` functions instead of `__builtin_isnan*`. GCC can't recognize or inline those, so `sklearn/tree/_partitioner.pyx`'s `isnan(value)` calls — sitting in the hottest loop of tree-building (`find_min_max`, `partition_samples`) — become genuine non-inlined function calls. This is `fit`-specific (confirmed: `predict`, which doesn't call these functions, shows no slowdown) and fully reproduced from source once the exact sysroot was pinned.


This is very likely **not scikit-learn-specific**: any conda-forge package with a hot-loop `isnan()`/`isinf()` call is plausibly exposed the same way.

~~=> TODO: Open an issue in conda-forge~~ Done: I posted a comment here: https://github.com/conda-forge/ctng-compiler-activation-feedstock/issues/108

### Proposed fix

Replace `from libc.math cimport isnan` / `isnan(value)` in `sklearn/tree/_partitioner.pyx` and `sklearn/tree/_utils.pxd` (and any other tree/HGB hot loop doing the same) with the self-inequality NaN test `value != value`. Pure comparison, nothing to inline, immune to this class of bug on any compiler/libc, forever.

### Root cause, in detail

*(pure LLM write-up)*

<details>

`sklearn/tree/_partitioner.pyx` (`DensePartitioner.find_min_max`, `.partition_samples`) and `sklearn/tree/_utils.pxd` call `isnan(value)` on `float32_t` data, via `from libc.math cimport isnan`. This runs once per sample per feature scan during `fit`; never during `predict`.

The feedstock's CI pin file (`.ci_support/linux_64_python3.12.____cpython.yaml` at the 1.9.0 release commit) sets `c_stdlib: sysroot`, `c_stdlib_version: '2.17'`. That sysroot's `math.h` has:

```c
#  define isnan(x) \
     (sizeof (x) == sizeof (float) ? __isnanf (x) \
      : sizeof (x) == sizeof (double) ? __isnan (x) : __isnanl (x))
```

Once the preprocessor expands this, the identifier `isnan` is gone from
the translation unit — GCC has nothing left to recognize as a builtin, so
`__isnanf` (an ordinary external glibc symbol, not a compiler intrinsic)
gets a real out-of-line call. Modern glibc instead defines `isnan(x)` as
`__builtin_isnan(x)` directly, which GCC folds to 2 instructions
(`ucomiss`/`setp`). PyPI/manylinux wheels don't hit this because they're
built with devtoolset-style toolchains: modern compiler *and* modern
headers, achieving old-system compatibility via glibc *symbol versioning*
at link time rather than by literally compiling against old headers.

Confirmed end to end:
- `perf`-profiled real installed PyPI vs conda-forge packages
  (`ExtraTreesRegressor.fit`, `n_features=30`): conda-forge spends 12.6% of
  samples in `__isnanf` alone; PyPI doesn't show it in the top 15 at all.
- Disassembled both real `.so` files directly: conda-forge's
  `find_min_max` has `call *0x1791f(%rip)  # <__isnanf@GLIBC_2.2.5>`;
  PyPI's has no call at all.
- Reproduced from source: rebuilding the actual v1.9.0 tag with the exact
  matching GCC (14.3.0-19, confirmed via the real binary's own
  `.comment` section) reproduced nothing *until* `sysroot_linux-64=2.17`
  was pinned explicitly (every environment had otherwise resolved the
  latest default, 2.39) — at which point the non-inlined call and the
  larger function size reappeared byte-for-byte.
- Same `isnan()` call pattern, same functions, confirmed still present on
  current `main` (the categorical-feature/Breiman-shortcut work added
  since 1.9.0 didn't touch this code path — `find_min_max` compiles to the
  identical byte size on both).

</details>

### Everything else that was tried and ruled out

Before finding the sysroot, a long list of variables was controlled for one at a time and **did not** reproduce the real-world gap when rebuilding from source with the real conda-forge `gcc_linux-64`/`gxx_linux-64` toolchain:

<details>

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.cluster import FeatureAgglomeration

X = np.random.RandomState(0).rand(10, 4)

fa.inverse_transform([[1.0, 2.0]])      # TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not tuple

fa.set_output(transform="pandas")
fa.inverse_transform(fa.transform(X))   # pandas InvalidIndexError
```

### Actual Results

- list: `TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not tuple`
- pandas (including the estimator's own `set_output(transform="pandas")` output): `InvalidIndexError` / `KeyError`
- polars: `DuplicateError`

A plain ndarray works.

```

Yes. I have a fix (validate with `check_array(X, ensure_2d=False)` in `inverse_transform`, plus tests for list/pandas/polars/1-D input) and would like to open the PR once this is triaged.

ARDRegression.scores_ combines updated precisions with the previous posterior

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

Hi, I’m Luis. I’m starting to contribute to scikit-learn by working through focused issues in its Bayesian linear models. I noticed this behavior while investigating `ARDRegression` after the discussion on #35026, and wanted to report a reproducible example before proposing a change.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

With `compute_score=True`, `ARDRegression` computes the posterior covariance and coefficients, updates `alpha_` and `lambda_`, then calculates `scores_` using the **updated precisions** but the **previous covariance and residual sum of squares**. As a result, the last score can differ from the objective evaluated at the fitted parameters. This can mislead users who inspect `scores_` to monitor optimization or compare the final score with an evaluation at the fitted parameters. Fitted coefficients and predictions appear unaffected

This is separate from whether the objective should include normalization constants: the comparison below omits the same constants as the current implementation.

If `scores_[-1]` is intended to report the objective at the fitted parameters, its covariance, coefficients, residuals, and precisions should correspond to the same parameter state.

There is also a related question for pruning: once the active feature set is stable, the determinant uses the covariance of retained features, while the score sums `log(lambda_)` over **all** features. Should the score represent evidence for the retained-feature model, or a limiting form of the full model? Clarifying that definition would help determine the appropriate treatment of pruned features.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import ARDRegression

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
X = rng.normal(size=(12, 4))
y = X @ np.array([1.2, -0.5, 0.0, 0.8]) + rng.normal(
    scale=0.3, size=12
)

reg = ARDRegression(
    max_iter=1,
    compute_score=True,
    fit_intercept=False,
    threshold_lambda=1e12,
    alpha_1=0.2,
    alpha_2=0.3,
    lambda_1=0.7,
    lambda_2=1.2,
).fit(X, y)

alpha, lam = reg.alpha_, reg.lambda_
A = np.diag(lam) + alpha * (X.T @ X)
mu = alpha * np.linalg.solve(A, X.T @ y)
sse = np.sum((y - X @ mu) ** 2)

score_at_fitted_parameters = (
    (reg.lambda_1 * np.log(lam) - reg.lambda_2 * lam).sum()
    + reg.alpha_1 * np.log(alpha)
    - reg.alpha_2 * alpha
    + 0.5 * (
        -np.linalg.slogdet(A)[1]
        + X.shape[0] * np.log(alpha)
        + np.log(lam).sum()
        - alpha * sse
        - np.sum(lam * mu**2)
    )
)

print(reg.scores_[-1])
print(score_at_fitted_parameters)
```

With scikit-learn 1.8.0, this prints approximately `-5.488435` and `-7.335993`. No features are pruned in this example. The calculations use the same unnormalized objective, so omitted constants do not explain the difference.

### Expected Results

The final `scores_` entry should equal the objective evaluated at the fitted `alpha_` and `lambda_`. For this reproducer, that value is approximately `-7.335993011208482`. Each score should use the posterior and precisions from the same iteration.

### Actual Results

With scikit-learn 1.8.0, the reproducer prints:

```text
-5.48843505092349
-7.335993011208482
```

The first value is `reg.scores_[-1]`; the second is the objective recomputed at the fitted parameters. They differ by approximately `1.847558`.

BUG: trees `fit(..., check_input=False)` silently ignores missing values

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`DecisionTree*.fit(X, y, check_input=False)` silently ignores missing values: with `check_input=False`, `_fit` skips `_compute_missing_values_in_feature_mask`, so `missing_values_in_feature_mask` stays `None` and the splitter treats NaNs as regular values. No error, no warning, just a wrong tree (NaN thresholds, spurious depth).

And there's no way around it from the public API: the mask can only be passed to the private `_fit`. That's what forests do (they compute the mask once and pass it to each tree via `tree._fit(..., check_input=False, missing_values_in_feature_mask=...)`).

Within scikit-learn, the only caller of the public `fit(..., check_input=False)` is `BaseGradientBoosting` (`_gb.py`), which is safe only because it rejects NaNs upfront. So this mostly affects third-party code using `check_input=False` (which the docstring discourages: "Don't use this parameter unless you know what you're doing").

More broadly, a single boolean isn't enough to express "this input was already validated" for trees anymore: callers also need to provide the missing-values mask (and, with categorical support, the encoding info). Possible ways forward:

1. **Compute the mask even when `check_input=False`** on the public `fit` (when none is provided). It's one pass over `X`, cheap compared to building a tree, and makes the result correct.
2. **Document** that missing values aren't supported with `check_input=False`. Cheap, but leaves a silent trap.
3. **Deprecate `check_input` in the public `fit`** of trees, and switch gradient boosting to `_fit` (like forests). With 1. applied during the deprecation cycle.

I'd go with 3.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X = np.array([[0.0], [1.0], [np.nan], [np.nan], [2.0], [3.0]], dtype=np.float32)
y = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0])

for check_input in (True, False):
    tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X, y, check_input=check_input)
    print(f"{check_input=}: depth={tree.get_depth()}, thresholds={tree.tree_.threshold}")
```

### Expected Results

Same tree for both (or at least an error for `check_input=False`):

```
check_input=True: depth=1, thresholds=[inf -2. -2.]
```

### Actual Results

```
check_input=True: depth=1, thresholds=[inf -2. -2.]
check_input=False: depth=4, thresholds=[nan nan -2. -2. nan -2. nan nan -2. -2. -2.]
```

BUG: `BaggingClassifier` with feature sub-sampling fails when routing `X_val` to `HistGradientBoosting*`

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.


### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Found while reviewing #34957.

`BaggingClassifier`/`BaggingRegressor` with `max_features < 1.0` (or `bootstrap_features=True`) fit each sub-estimator on `X[:, features]`, but they forward routed metadata as-is. So when `X_val` is routed to `HistGradientBoosting*`, the sub-estimator gets a full-width `X_val` while it was fitted on a subset of columns, and it raises:

```
ValueError: X has 20 features, but HistGradientBoostingClassifier is expecting 10 features as input.
```

The root cause is more general than Bagging: routers treat metadata as opaque, and only know how to slice "sample-aligned" metadata on rows (`_check_method_params`). They have no notion of "feature-aligned" metadata like `X_val`, which should get the same column selection as `X`. This seems closely related to #34270 (declaring metadata properties to be used by the routers).

With #34957, `X_val`/`y_val` will be auto-requested, so users will hit this more easily (no explicit `set_fit_request` needed).

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier, HistGradientBoostingClassifier

sklearn.set_config(enable_metadata_routing=True)

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=500, n_features=20, random_state=0)
X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val = X[:400], y[:400], X[400:], y[400:]

    X_val=True, y_val=True
)
bagging = BaggingClassifier(hgb, max_features=0.5, random_state=0)
bagging.fit(X_train, y_train, X_val=X_val, y_val=y_val)
```

`from sklearn.model_selection import *` raises ImportError since 1.8.0

### Introduce yourself

Hi, I'm a CS student and regular scikit-learn user, mostly through model_selection. I ran into this while star-importing the module in a notebook and traced it back to a specific commit. First time filing a bug here.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`from sklearn.model_selection import *` raises an ImportError on 1.8.0+. It worked in 1.7.2, and every other public submodule still star-imports fine.

The cause: `HalvingGridSearchCV` and `HalvingRandomSearchCV` are listed in `__all__` (in `sklearn/model_selection/__init__.py`), but the module's `__getattr__` deliberately raises ImportError for both until you import `enable_halving_search_cv`. Star-import pulls every name in `__all__`, so it hits that guard and fails. The two names were added to `__all__` in #31847 (the ruff absolute-imports cleanup); before that they weren't exported.

Impact: any notebook or script doing `from sklearn.model_selection import *` breaks on upgrade to 1.8.0, with an error that looks unrelated to what the user actually did.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import *
```

Star-import succeeds like it did in 1.7.2, without exporting the experimental Halving classes.

### Actual Results

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
  File ".../sklearn/model_selection/__init__.py", line 100, in __getattr__
    raise ImportError(
ImportError: HalvingGridSearchCV is experimental and the API might change without any deprecation cycle. To use it, you need to explicitly import enable_halving_search_cv:
from sklearn.experimental import enable_halving_search_cv
```

```shell
System:
    python: 3.12.10 (tags/v3.12.10:0cc8128, Apr  8 2025, 12:21:36) [MSC v.1943 64 bit (AMD64)]
   machine: Windows-11-10.0.26200-SP0

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.10.dev0

        numpy: 2.6.0.dev0
        scipy: 2.0.0.dev0

threadpoolctl: 3.7.0

Also reproduces on 1.8.0.
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Happy to open a PR. Plan: drop the two names from `__all__` and keep them in the `TYPE_CHECKING` import with `# noqa: F401`, the way 1.7.2 had it.

BUG: Explicit validation data does not enable HistGradientBoosting automatic early stopping

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

_No response_

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`HistGradientBoostingRegressor` and `HistGradientBoostingClassifier` accept explicit `X_val` and `y_val` but do not enable early stopping with `early_stopping="auto"` on a small training set. This also affects calls that leave `early_stopping` at its default value, `"auto"`.

In the example below, both estimators fit successfully on 30 training samples, but `do_early_stopping_` is `False` and `validation_score_` is empty. Changing only `early_stopping` to `True` enables monitoring of the same validation data and records four validation scores.

The user-facing problem is that the supplied validation data does not participate in the early-stopping checks, despite the documented automatic activation. This is not just missing score history: the validation-based stopping criterion is disabled. In longer runs, this could cause unnecessary boosting iterations and potentially affect generalization. The example establishes disabled monitoring and stopping checks; it does not establish degraded predictions or a production incident.

A workaround is to set `early_stopping=True` explicitly when providing validation arrays.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import sklearn
from sklearn.ensemble import (
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
    HistGradientBoostingRegressor,
)

print(sklearn.__version__)
X = np.arange(40.0).reshape(-1, 1)

for estimator_class in (
    HistGradientBoostingRegressor,
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
):
    y = (
        np.sin(X[:, 0])
        if estimator_class is HistGradientBoostingRegressor
        else np.arange(40) % 2
    )
    for mode in ("auto", True):
        estimator = estimator_class(
            early_stopping=mode, max_iter=3, random_state=0
        ).fit(X[:30], y[:30], X_val=X[30:], y_val=y[30:])
        print(
            estimator_class.__name__, mode,
            estimator.do_early_stopping_,
            len(estimator.validation_score_),
        )
```

### Expected Results

With explicit validation arrays, both modes should enable early stopping for both estimators, even with only 30 training samples:

```text
1.9.0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor auto True 4
HistGradientBoostingRegressor True True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier auto True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier True True 4
```

The version 1.9 documentation specifies automatic activation when either the training sample count exceeds 10,000 or `X_val` and `y_val` are supplied to `fit`:

- [HistGradientBoostingRegressor documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingRegressor.html)
- [HistGradientBoostingClassifier documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/1.9/modules/generated/sklearn.ensemble.HistGradientBoostingClassifier.html)

Four scores correspond to the initial model plus three completed boosting iterations. The example tests whether validation monitoring is enabled, not whether fitting must terminate before `max_iter`.

### Actual Results

The reported run on scikit-learn 1.9.0 produced:

```text
1.9.0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor auto False 0
HistGradientBoostingRegressor True True 4
HistGradientBoostingClassifier auto False 0
HistGradientBoostingClassifier True True 4
```

No exception is raised. Automatic mode leaves early stopping disabled and records no validation scores, while explicit `True` monitors the same validation data.

### Versions

```shell
1.9.0
1.9.1
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

In [`BaseHistGradientBoosting.fit` at tag 1.9.0](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/1.9.0/sklearn/ensemble/_hist_gradient_boosting/gradient_boosting.py), the automatic-mode decision only checks the training sample count:

```python
if self.early_stopping == "auto":
    self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000
```

The method has already calculated `validation_data_provided` and checked that both validation arrays are supplied together, but that flag is not included in the automatic-mode decision.

A candidate fix is:

```diff
- self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000
+ self.do_early_stopping_ = n_samples > 10_000 or validation_data_provided
```

This is a source-based suggestion, not a tested patch.

A regression test should cover both estimator classes with a small training set, explicit validation arrays, and `early_stopping="auto"`, and check:

```python
assert estimator.do_early_stopping_
assert len(estimator.validation_score_) == estimator.n_iter_ + 1
```

Keep `early_stopping=True` as a passing control. Additional coverage should preserve the sample-count rule when validation arrays are absent, including the 10,000-sample boundary, and preserve the existing validation-argument errors.

Related work: [#18748](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/18748) requested custom validation-set support, and [#27124](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/27124) introduced the explicit validation arguments. These references do not establish that no duplicate report exists.
